source.title: Towards Robustness to Label Noise in Text Classification via Noise Modeling
source.authors: Siddhant Garg; Goutham Ramakrishnan; Varun Thumbe

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Some table formatting is flattened, but the model, method, noise level, and accuracy entries in Tables 1, 3, and 4 are recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests training on datasets with corrupted labels, but reports clean test accuracy and a best-to-last test-accuracy gap rather than training error or time to fit random labels. This is a different measure of noisy-label learning.
record.gate_note: The paper injects random label noise at 10–50% and reports results in Table 1. It does not report training error on corrupted examples, so it cannot establish perfect fitting of random labels. It also reports input-conditional noise in Tables 3 and 4; those conditions are outside V4's random-corruption sweep. No results address shuffled or noise inputs, regularization removal, or learning order.
record.test_reason: Figure 2 reports the study's own training-loss trajectories for a word-LSTM on TREC with 40% random label noise: clean-label losses fall before noisy-label losses, and both become low later. This directly tests V6 in a text-classification setting, beyond merely using that finding for denoising. Table 1 also bears on V4's test-performance component.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct: the authors conclude that jointly training a classifier and auxiliary noise model with a denoising loss can improve text-classification accuracy and reduce overfitting to label noise. Benefits vary by dataset and noise type, with weaker mitigation for input-conditional noise.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an auxiliary noise model, a beta-mixture model to estimate clean-label probabilities, and a de-noising loss. It tests text classification with partial label corruption and evaluates clean test accuracy; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, noise type, and noise level affect the reported accuracy and best-to-last test-accuracy gap. The authors state the method is more effective on TREC than AG-News; results also differ between random and input-conditional noise.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed denoising methods improve clean test accuracy in many conditions and reduce the best-to-last test-accuracy gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Auxiliary noise modeling can improve robustness to corrupted training labels in text classification.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’21)
record.problems: The paper reports clean test accuracy and the difference between last and best test accuracy, not training error on corrupted labels. Noise is artificially injected, and the random-noise sweep covers 10–50% rather than 0–100%. Results are reported for two text datasets and two architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: Table 1 reports clean test accuracy and best-to-last test-accuracy differences, which do not measure whether the models fit corrupted training labels perfectly. Tables 3 and 4 report input-conditional noise results and likewise do not measure training-set fitting.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fitting throughout the corruption sweep and degradation through 100% corruption to chance. Table 1 supplies clean baselines and 10–50% noise results, but no training-error measurements.
Comparisons with and without explicit regularization, including its effects on random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
Whether the illustrated learning order extends across other architectures, datasets, and corruption levels; Figure 2 directly illustrates only word-LSTM on TREC with 40% random noise.

missing.what: Clean-versus-noisy training-loss distributions at epochs 1, 9, and 30 for word-LSTM on TREC with 40% random noise. These directly demonstrate learning order and are neither extracted nor declared in rows_left_out. Record the qualitative loss separation and subsequent reduction; do not infer exact training accuracy from these histograms.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly says no results address learning order: Figure 2 does. Table 1's baseline test accuracies bear on V4's degradation component, although they cannot establish perfect training fitting; those results are already explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing here and receive no row-based verdict. The record also incorrectly calls the 0% endpoint unavailable: clean baseline accuracies appear beside the dataset headings. Section 4.1's example says 30% noise, but its numbers—79.6 with a 24.8-point drop and 83.4 with a 1.0-point drop—belong to 40% noise in Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: Training error on completely random labels, test error at chance, and whether architecture or training hyperparameters must change.
Training time or convergence speed for random versus true labels, including change with corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper reports test accuracy at 10–50% random label noise, but does not report training-set fitting error, 0% and 100% noise endpoints, or a complete test-error trend from none to all corruption. Table 1 results are not extracted as rows because the reported test-accuracy metric alone cannot determine whether training labels were fit perfectly.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or whether learning proceeds differently over training.

relationships.condition: Word-LSTM on TREC with 40% random label noise, trained with cross-entropy.
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict from Figure 2 and Section 3.1; missing rows: losses are initially high for both groups, lower for clean samples at epoch 9, and low for both groups at epoch 30, demonstrating clean-label learning before noise memorization.
relationships.display_finding: Losses were initially high for both groups, lower for clean samples at epoch 9, and low for both groups at epoch 30.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
